question: Ten years on from the Bataclan, the proliferation of Islamist terrorist attacks highlights the critical shortcomings of the EU’s approach to immigration
Last month marked the ten-year anniversary of the 13 November Islamist terror attacks in Paris, which left 130 people dead.

A number of Member States have, in the last few years, witnessed a dramatic increase in the number of threats, violent acts and terror attacks connected to Islamist groups, proof that radical Islam still constitutes a significant threat and is thriving in marginalised communities and as a result of the failure to effectively manage integration and immigration.

According to Europol’s TE-SAT 2025 Report1, the EU was hit by 58 terror attacks across 14 Member States in 2024 alone. Of these, 24 were attributed to Islamist groups and resulted in the deaths of 5 people and the wounding of 18 more. In addition, 289 arrests were made that year in connection with jihadist activities.

The joint Europol-Interpol report on migrant smuggling networks2 highlights that more than 90 % of irregular immigrants use criminal networks that are often employed by arms smugglers and by foreign fighters wishing to return to the EU.

In short, the number of Islamist terror attacks has multiplied in the ten years since the Bataclan attack, testament to the shortcomings of the EU’s immigration and integration policies. In the light of the above: 1.
Is the Commission planning to revise the EU’s immigration model?
What measures will it take to combat Islamist terrorism and mitigate the threat to the security and stability of the Union?
Is it planning to step up checks at the EU’s borders to identify radicalised immigrants and, if so, what operational and preventive tools will it employ?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.3.2026) The Pact on Migration and Asylum1 overhauls the migration and asylum system, providing for more control over illegal migration, simplifying rules and procedures on asylum, strengthening resilience and preparedness, and introducing instruments for managing crises.

In January 2026, the Commission presented the European Asylum and Migration Management Strategy2 outlining concrete priorities for the next five years, including preventing illegal migration. The Commission is staying vigilant regarding terrorism and violent extremism and will present the new ProtectEU: Agenda to prevent and counter terrorism on 26 February 2026.

This Agenda will detail key actions for the EU institutions, Member States, EU agencies and private sector to better anticipate threats, prevent radicalisation, protect people both online and offline, respond effectively to attacks, and strengthen international cooperation. The Commission is working closely with Member States to protect the external borders.

All persons entering and exiting the Schengen area undergo systematic checks in the Schengen Information System. The Entry/Exit System, the future European Travel Authorisation System and the revised Visa Information System will allow for the cross-checking of travellers against EU databases and the pre-assessing of security risks posed by third-country nationals.

Under the Schengen Borders Code3, Member States must ensure an efficient, high and uniform level of controls at external borders and carry out systematic checks. From June 2026, the new Screening Regulation4 will require Member States to carry out in-depth security checks on all persons crossing external borders outside border crossing points.
